blocks.text: Disappointed, K. took the letter and put it in his pocket. Even in the most favourable case, the advantage the recommendation could bring him was comparatively smaller than the harm done by the manufacturer's knowing of his trial and the painter's spreading the news further. He could scarcely bring himself to thank the manufacturer, who was already on his way to the door, in a few words. “I shall go there,” he said as he took leave of the manufacturer at the door, “or, since I am very busy just now, write and ask him to come to my office some time.” “I knew, of course,” said the manufacturer, “that you would find the best way out. I did think, however, that you would prefer to avoid inviting people like this Titorelli to the bank to speak with him here about the trial. Nor is it always advisable to let letters to such people pass out of one's hands. But you have surely thought everything over and know what you may venture to do.” K. nodded and accompanied the manufacturer through the anteroom. Yet despite his outward composure he was greatly alarmed at himself. He had really only said that he would write to Titorelli in order to show the manufacturer somehow that he appreciated the recommendation and was at once considering the possibilities of meeting Titorelli, but if he had regarded Titorelli's assistance as valuable, he would not have hesitated actually to write to him. Yet it was only through the manufacturer's remark that he had recognized the dangers this might entail. Could he truly rely so little on his own judgement already? If it was possible for him to invite a dubious person to the bank by an explicit letter, in order to ask his advice about his trial, separated from the deputy manager by only a door, was it not possible and even very probable that he was overlooking other dangers too, or rushing into them? There was not always someone standing beside him to warn him. And just now, when he meant to act with all his strength mustered, such doubts about his own vigilance, hitherto unknown to him, had to arise! Were the difficulties he felt in carrying out his office work now to begin in the trial as well? Now, indeed, he could no longer understand at all how it had been possible for him to want to write to Titorelli and invite him to the bank.

He was still shaking his head over it when the attendant came to his side and drew his attention to three gentlemen sitting on a bench here in the anteroom. They had been waiting a long time to be admitted to K. Now that the attendant was speaking to K., they had risen, and each wished to seize a favourable opportunity to approach K. before the others. Since the bank was so inconsiderate as to let them waste their time here in the waiting room, they too were no longer disposed to show consideration. “Sir,” one of them was already saying. But K. had asked the attendant to bring his winter overcoat, and as he put it on with the attendant's help he said to all three: “Forgive me, gentlemen, unfortunately I have no time to receive you at present. I beg your pardon, but I have an urgent matter of business to attend to and must leave at once. You have seen for yourselves how long I have just been detained. Would you be so kind as to come again tomorrow, or whenever it suits you? Or shall we perhaps discuss these matters by telephone? Or perhaps you would care to tell me briefly now what it is about, and I shall then give you a full reply in writing. It would be best, though, if you came again before long.” These proposals of K.'s so astonished the gentlemen, whose waiting was now to have been entirely in vain, that they looked at one another in silence. “Then we are agreed?” asked K., who had turned towards the attendant, who was now bringing him his hat as well. Through the open door to K.'s room one could see that the snowfall outside had grown much heavier. K. therefore turned up his coat collar and buttoned it high beneath his chin.
